module_title: Mechanics I - Kinematics and NLM (Basic / Foundational)
introduction: This foundational level covers the core principles of one-dimensional motion and Newton's basic laws. It serves as the bedrock for all subsequent physics topics in NEET and JEE. Mastery here ensures you can track the position, velocity, and acceleration of an object, as well as understand the basic forces acting upon it.

core_concepts.title: Distance vs. Displacement
core_concepts.description: Distance is the total path covered (scalar), while displacement is the shortest straight-line distance between initial and final positions (vector). Displacement can be zero or negative, but distance is always positive.

core_concepts.title: Equations of Motion (Constant Acceleration)
core_concepts.description: The three fundamental equations are: v = u + at, s = ut + 0.5at^2, and v^2 = u^2 + 2as. These are strictly applicable only when acceleration (a) remains constant.

core_concepts.title: Newton's First Law (Inertia)
core_concepts.description: An object will remain at rest or in uniform motion in a straight line unless acted upon by an external, unbalanced force. Inertia is directly proportional to mass.

core_concepts.title: Newton's Second Law (F = ma)
core_concepts.description: The rate of change of momentum of a body is directly proportional to the applied force. For a constant mass, this simplifies to Force = mass x acceleration.

core_concepts.title: Newton's Third Law (Action-Reaction)
core_concepts.description: To every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction. Crucially, action and reaction forces act on two different bodies, not the same body.

important_entities.name: Free Body Diagram (FBD)
important_entities.key_fact: Visual isolation of a single body.
important_entities.significance: The most critical tool for solving NLM problems. It maps out all external forces acting purely on the chosen object to easily write F=ma equations.

important_entities.name: Inertial Frame of Reference
important_entities.significance: Newton's laws of motion are strictly valid only in inertial frames of reference (e.g., ground, a car moving at constant velocity).

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Average speed is total distance/total time. Average velocity is total displacement/total time. If a particle returns to its starting point, its average velocity is 0, but its average speed is strictly positive. Do not just average the two velocities (v1+v2)/2 unless time intervals are exactly equal.

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: Down to Differentiate, Up to Integrate
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: To go from Displacement (S) to Velocity (V) to Acceleration (A), you differentiate with respect to time. To go backwards (A to V to S), you integrate.

exam_strategy_tips: Always define your positive and negative sign conventions before plugging numbers into the equations of motion (e.g., taking upward as positive and gravity as -g).
Direct graph-reading questions (Area under v-t graph = displacement; Slope of v-t graph = acceleration) are highly frequent in NEET.
